examples.title: Power laws in the doctoral-advisor network
examples.description: Wikidata's 408,000 doctoral supervisions (P184): students per advisor are heavy-tailed (7 advisors with 100+ students, where a same-mean geometric expects 10⁻¹⁰), advisors per student are not. Fitting a power law the right way (Clauset, Shalizi & Newman): CCDF instead of histogram, maximum-likelihood α, x_min by KS distance, Vuong's likelihood-ratio test against an exponential. Caveats: Wikidata coverage bias; lognormal not fitted.

catalog.title: Power laws in the doctoral-advisor network

catalog.description: Question: do a few advisors collect most doctoral students, and is it a power law? Wikidata's doctoral-advisor relation gives 118,046 advisors and 334,857 students. Half the advisors have one recorded student, but 7 have 100 or more, which a same-mean geometric puts at 10⁻¹⁰. The dashboard plots the CCDF, fits α by maximum likelihood over a KS-chosen x_min, and tests it against an exponential with Vuong's likelihood ratio. Students per advisor are heavy-tailed but bend (α goes from 1.7 to 4.0 as x_min rises), and in the tail the power law can't be told from an exponential; advisors per student are exponential. Caveats: Wikidata coverage bias, lognormal not fitted.

examples.title: Benford's law in country statistics
examples.description: Population, land area, GDP and CO₂ emissions of every country from the World Bank, and the first significant digit of each. Statistics idea: Benford's law: quantities spanning several orders of magnitude start with 1 about 30% of the time and with 9 under 5% (log10(1 + 1/d)); a chi-square test and the mean absolute deviation say how close each comes. Caveats: ~215 countries is a small sample for a digit test, values are each country's latest year, and conformity is not proof of honest numbers.

examples.title: The C-value paradox: genome size against gene number
examples.description: 1,000 annotated reference genomes (NCBI Datasets) of bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants and animals. Genes scale with genome size in bacteria (b = 1.01, about 900 genes per Mb) but hardly in animals (b = 0.15) or plants (0.26): most of a big genome is not genes. Caveats: NCBI's first 200 per group, annotation-dependent counts.

catalog.title: The C-value paradox: genome size against gene number
catalog.summary: 1,000 NCBI reference genomes: genes scale 1:1 with size in bacteria, barely at all in plants and animals (b 0.15–0.26).
catalog.description: Question: does a bigger genome mean more genes? If DNA were mostly genes, gene count would grow in proportion to genome size (genes ∝ size^b with b = 1). Data: 1,000 annotated reference genomes from NCBI Datasets, the first 200 of each of five groups (bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants, animals): assembly size, G+C % and protein-coding gene count. Steps: per genome the size in Mb and the gene density (genes per Mb); per group a least-squares fit of log10(genes) on log10(size), whose slope b is the scaling exponent, with R², and the fold ranges of size and gene count; the same for prokaryotes against eukaryotes. Aha: in bacteria b = 1.01 (R² 0.99) and archaea 0.88: a prokaryote genome is genes packed end to end, about 900–1,000 per Mb at any size. In eukaryotes the law breaks: animal genomes span a 500-fold range of size (57 Mb to the axolotl's 29 Gb) with b = 0.15, plants 0.26, fungi 0.53, and the median density falls to 25 genes per Mb in animals. Genome size says little about gene number or complexity: the C-value paradox. The extra DNA is introns, repeats and transposable elements, which this data does not hold. Caveats: NCBI's first 200 reference genomes per group are a sample in NCBI's order, not random, and over-represent well-studied species; gene counts depend on the annotation pipeline (RefSeq or submitter), and polyploids (wheat, 104k genes) count every copy; assembly length is not flow-cytometry C-value (repeats may be missing from assemblies); microsporidia (Encephalitozoon) count as fungi. Next: hover a genome; drill down to one group (insects, grasses: any NCBI taxon id in the same query); expand to repeat content or intron length, or to Lynch's population-size hypothesis.

examples.title: Caffeine in its receptor
examples.description: Caffeine bound in its real target, the human adenosine A2A receptor (RCSB 5MZP, 2.1 Å), in 3D, against adenosine, the agonist it blocks (2YDO). Contacts are computed from the coordinates: per residue within 5 Å, an H-bond candidate (N/O under 3.5 Å), π-stacking (ring centroids within 5.5 Å) or hydrophobic (C–C under 4 Å), with GPCRdb helix positions and UniProt binding sites. Idea: a molecule blocks a receptor by fitting its pocket without activating it: caffeine keeps adenosine's purine contacts (stacking on Phe168, an H-bond to Asn253) but, with no ribose, none of the ribose contacts (Ser277, His278) agonists use. Caveats: static snapshots of thermostabilised, mutated receptors (5MZP has Ala at 88 and 277); distance cutoffs, not energies or affinity; A1 is a caffeine target too.

examples.title: Die yield: why big chips are expensive and chiplets exist
examples.description: Real die areas from Wikidata (Apple A-series to M1 Max, console APUs, GPUs, camera sensors) under Poisson, Murphy and negative-binomial yield models. Idea: yield falls exponentially with area, so a good mm² of a big die costs more, and splitting into tested chiplets recovers it. Caveats: defect densities and the chiplet overhead are scenarios; few die areas on Wikidata.

catalog.title: Die yield: why big chips are expensive and chiplets exist
catalog.summary: Real die areas under Poisson, Murphy and negative-binomial yield: big dies lose exponentially, and tested chiplets win the silicon back.
catalog.description: Question: why does a chip twice the size cost more than twice as much, and why did AMD, Intel and Apple start building processors from several small dies (chiplets)? Data: every chip and image sensor on Wikidata with a die area in mm² (SPARQL, keyless): Apple's A4 to M1 Max, AMD's APUs, console chips, Radeon GPUs, and camera sensors up to full frame (864 mm²). Steps: gross dies per 300 mm wafer, π(d/2)²/A − πd/√(2A); the share that works under three defect models (Poisson e^(−A·D0), Murphy's, and the negative binomial for clustered defects) for defect densities of 0.05 to 0.5 per cm²; the silicon cost of a good mm² against an ideal die; and the same designs split into 2, 4 or 8 tested chiplets, each 10% larger than its share. Aha: yield falls exponentially with area, so the cost of a good mm² climbs steeply for big dies, worst on a young process: splitting a big die into chiplets that are tested before packaging recovers most of the lost silicon, which is why big chips are now built from small ones. Caveats: the defect densities are scenarios (foundries publish few), not data, and so are the 300 mm wafer and the 10% interface overhead; Wikidata has die areas for a few dozen chips only and some entries may be package or sensor areas; packaging, test, interconnect yield and the scribe lines are ignored; real fabs also repair dies with spare cores and memory rows. Next: drill into one die (click it for Wikipedia), expand to wafer prices per node and to published D0 figures (TSMC's N5 ramp), or to the transistor count each die holds (chip-moore-dennard).

examples.title: Direct and indirect band gaps: why LEDs are not silicon
examples.description: Every stable element and binary compound with a gap in Alexandria (PBE) by family, from PubChem valences. Idea: an indirect gap needs a phonon to emit light; Si sits 1.9 eV above the direct line, GaAs, InP, GaN and Zn/Cd chalcogenides on it. Shares per family with Wilson intervals and a two-proportion test. Caveats: PBE gaps are 30–100% too small (Ge, InAs missing), small families.

catalog.title: Direct and indirect band gaps: why LEDs are not silicon
catalog.summary: Stable semiconductors by family: silicon's gap is indirect, GaAs, GaN and InP are direct, which is why LEDs and lasers are III-V or II-VI.
catalog.description: Question: why are LEDs and laser diodes made of III-V and II-VI compounds (GaAs, InP, GaN, ZnSe) and not of silicon, the best-understood semiconductor there is? Data: every stable element and binary compound with a band gap and at most 4 atoms per cell in Alexandria (PBE density-functional calculations, Ruhr University Bochum, via its keyless OPTIMADE API): the fundamental gap and the smallest direct gap; and PubChem's periodic table for each element's valence electrons and electronegativity. Steps: the gap is direct when the smallest vertical gap equals the fundamental one (within 0.005 eV); each material gets a family from its elements' valences (III-V: 3 and 5 in a 1:1 compound; II-VI and I-VII split by whether the metal has a full d shell, Zn/Cd/Hg and Cu/Ag, or is an alkaline-earth/alkali metal); shares of direct gaps per family with Wilson 95% intervals; a two-proportion z-test of III-V and II-VI against the rest. Aha: an electron in an indirect-gap material (Si: the direct gap is about 1.9 eV above the fundamental one) can only fall across the gap if a lattice vibration takes up its momentum, so it emits light a million times more slowly than it loses its energy as heat; in GaAs or GaN the band edges line up and a photon is emitted directly. Caveats: PBE underestimates band gaps by 30 to 100% (Si 0.65 eV here against 1.12 measured; GaAs 0.20 against 1.42), and Ge, InAs and InSb come out metallic and are missing; the direct/indirect character is more robust than the value but near-direct materials (GaP, margin 0.02 eV) can flip; families with few members have wide intervals; the photon wavelengths in the tooltips use PBE gaps and are too long. Next: drill into III-V (why AlAs and GaP are indirect), expand to alloys (AlGaAs, GaAsP turn indirect at a crossover composition) and to measured gaps.

examples.title: Moore's law and the end of Dennard scaling
examples.description: Fifty years of CPUs (Karl Rupp's trend data): transistors, clock, power, single-thread performance and cores on a log scale. Idea: a constant doubling time is a straight line in log2; the clock's best break year (2004) splits each trend, and a Chow test and Dennard's power budget (P ≈ N·C·V²·f) show transistors kept doubling every ~2 years while the clock and power went flat. Caveats: pre-2010 points digitised from a plot, high-end CPUs only, break chosen on the clock data.

catalog.title: Moore's law and the end of Dennard scaling
catalog.summary: Fifty years of CPUs: transistors kept doubling every ~2 years, but the clock and power went flat after 2004, the end of Dennard scaling.
catalog.description: Question: transistors kept doubling for fifty years, so why did clock speed stop rising around 2005, and where did the extra transistors go? Data: Karl Rupp's microprocessor trend data (CC BY 4.0; transistors, clock, typical power, single-thread SpecINT and logical cores for about 100 CPUs, 1971–2021). Steps: each measure as log2 of its value against year, so a straight line is a constant doubling time; for the clock, a two-line fit for every candidate break year from 1995 to 2014 (the year with the smallest squared error wins); each measure fitted before and after that year with 95% intervals; a Chow F-test of one line against two; and Dennard's budget: dynamic power P ≈ N·C·V²·f, so the doublings per year of transistors × clock minus those of power is how fast the switching energy C·V² had to fall. Aha: the transistor line barely bends at the break, but the clock and power lines go flat: until the mid-2000s each shrink lowered the voltage, paying for faster clocks at constant power density (Dennard scaling); when leakage stopped the voltage from falling, the clock froze at the cooling limit and the extra transistors became cores. Caveats: points before 2010 were digitised from a published plot (Horowitz, Labonte, Shacham, Olukotun, Hammond, Batten), later ones collected by Rupp; the sample is high-end Intel/AMD/IBM CPUs, not phones or GPUs; power is TDP; the break year is chosen on the clock data, so the clock's Chow p-value is optimistic; each file's first line (the 1971 Intel 4004) is read as a CSV header and dropped. Next: the voltage data that would test the mechanism (in the study), die area for power density, and Rupp's blog post for the story.

examples.title: Why semiconductors are tetrahedral: the Mooser–Pearson map
examples.description: Octet AB compounds (Alexandria ground states, PubChem electronegativities) on Δχ against mean principal quantum number. Idea: covalent bonds between light atoms are tetrahedral (zincblende, wurtzite), ionic ones rock salt; one Δχ threshold sorts 87%, Fisher's line 91%. Caveats: Pauling Δχ is a crude ionicity; PBE puts Li halides in wurtzite.

catalog.title: Why semiconductors are tetrahedral: the Mooser–Pearson map
catalog.summary: Octet compounds on electronegativity difference against atom size: covalent and light means four neighbours (zincblende), ionic means rock salt.
catalog.description: Question: silicon, GaAs, GaN, ZnSe, SiC: why is every semiconductor in a chip built of atoms with exactly four neighbours, while table salt and magnesium oxide, made of the same kinds of elements, take six? Data: every stable binary AB compound in Alexandria (PBE ground states, keyless OPTIMADE) with 2 or 4 atoms per cell made of main-group and d10 elements, and PubChem's periodic table for valence electrons, electronegativity and period. Steps: keep the octet compounds (two atoms bringing 8 valence electrons: I-VII, II-VI, III-V, IV-IV); read the coordination from the ground-state space group (zincblende and wurtzite 4, rock salt 6, CsCl 8); place each on the Mooser–Pearson map (Pauling electronegativity difference Δχ against the mean principal quantum number n̄); find the best single Δχ threshold and Fisher's linear discriminant on both, and their accuracy against always guessing the larger class. Aha: the structure is predictable from two atomic numbers: covalent bonds between light atoms (small Δχ, small n̄) are directional sp³ bonds pointing to four neighbours, the open tetrahedral network that gives a band gap with mobile carriers; ionic bonds (large Δχ) are not directional and pack six neighbours. One number already does most of the work: Δχ below about 1.3 predicts four neighbours for 87% of the compounds (against 52% for always guessing the larger class), and adding n̄ (Fisher's line) gets 91%. ZnO and BeO stay tetrahedral at quite large Δχ because their atoms are small, MgO and CdO go rock salt. Caveats: Pauling's Δχ is a crude ionicity (Phillips' spectroscopic ionicity from optical data separates the two classes completely at 0.785, but needs dielectric constants not fetched here); ground states are PBE at zero temperature and pressure (energy differences of a few meV/atom can flip: PBE puts LiCl, LiBr and LiI in wurtzite, while they crystallise as rock salt, and those three are most of the line's misses); no IV-IV compound (SiC) is in the ground-state set with these cell sizes; compounds with larger cells are left out; the discriminant is fitted and judged on the same compounds. Next: drill into the misclassified compounds (scored table), expand to Phillips ionicity with dielectric data, or to how pressure turns tetrahedral semiconductors into rock salt.

examples.title: Vegard's law and lattice matching for epitaxy
examples.description: III-V binaries and ordered (In,Ga)As and (Al,Ga)As cells (Alexandria, PBE) with measured cells (COD). Idea: an alloy's lattice constant is linear in composition (Vegard), its gap bows; solving for InP gives In0.53Ga0.47As with measured cells (0.47 with PBE). Caveats: PBE lattice constants 1–2% large and gaps far too small; ordered, not random, alloys.

catalog.title: Vegard's law and lattice matching for epitaxy
catalog.summary: Alloy lattice constants are linear in composition, so In0.53Ga0.47As fits InP: the gap-against-lattice-constant map of III-V epitaxy.
catalog.description: Question: how do you grow a perfect crystal of one semiconductor on a wafer of another, and why is the photodetector in every fibre-optic receiver made of exactly In0.53Ga0.47As? Data: Alexandria's PBE calculations (keyless OPTIMADE) of the zincblende III-V binaries, Si and Ge, and of ordered (In,Ga)As and (Al,Ga)As cells; measured lattice constants of GaAs, InAs, AlAs and InP from the Crystallography Open Database. Steps: the cubic lattice constant from each cell's volume (a = (8V/atoms)^(1/3)); each alloy against the straight line between its end points (Vegard's law) and a least-squares bowing parameter for its lattice constant and band gap; the composition x* where In(x)Ga(1−x)As has InP's lattice constant, from PBE and from measured values; PBE's error against the measured cells. Aha: an alloy's lattice constant is linear in its composition (the ordered alloys sit on Vegard's line to a few hundredths of a percent) while its band gap bends, so composition is a dial: pick x to match the substrate, then the gap follows; on the gap-against-lattice-constant map every epitaxial stack is a vertical line, GaAs and AlAs share one (strain-free AlGaAs lasers and transistors), and InP's crosses (In,Ga)As at x ≈ 0.53. Caveats: PBE lattice constants are 1–2% too large and not uniformly so, which moves the matched x (0.47 with PBE, 0.53 with the measured cells) and even flips the sign of the tiny AlAs-on-GaAs mismatch (−0.21% PBE, +0.13% measured); PBE gaps are far too small (InAs and the In-rich alloys have none), so the gap axis is qualitative; ordered cells are not random alloys and fold the indirect valleys onto Γ; strain, critical thickness and thermal-expansion mismatch are not computed. Next: drill into one alloy's cells (click), expand to (Ga,In)P on GaAs, GaN on sapphire or SiGe on Si, and to critical thickness.

examples.title: Bragg's law and the selection rules of semiconductor crystals
examples.description: Simulated Cu Kα powder patterns of Si, Ge, diamond, GaAs, AlAs and InP from COD cell edges. Idea: Bragg's law plus the structure factor of a two-atom fcc basis: (200) is extinct in Si, faint in GaAs, strong in InP; a film's peak splitting grows as tan θ. Caveats: scattering factors approximated by Z, no thermal motion.

catalog.title: Bragg's law and the selection rules of semiconductor crystals
catalog.summary: Powder patterns of Si, Ge, GaAs, AlAs and InP from COD cells: (200) is extinct in Si, faint in GaAs, strong in InP; film peaks split as tan θ.
catalog.description: Question: how does an X-ray diffractometer tell silicon from gallium arsenide, and how does it measure a film a few nanometres thick on a wafer? Data: the Crystallography Open Database's entries for Si, Ge, C, GaAs, AlAs and InP (keyless JSON), the cubic cell edge a of each (the entry nearest the median of its cubic entries), and PubChem's atomic numbers. Steps: Bragg's law nλ = 2d sin θ with d = a/√(h²+k²+l²) for Cu Kα1 (1.5406 Å); the structure factor of an fcc lattice with a two-atom basis (|F|² = 16(f_A ± f_B)² or 16(f_A² + f_B²) by the parity of h, k, l); intensities with multiplicity and the Lorentz-polarisation factor; and the splitting between a film's and a substrate's peaks, Δ2θ ≈ −2 tan θ · Δa/a. Aha: the (200) reflection is extinct in Si, Ge and diamond (one kind of atom, so the two atoms of the basis cancel), almost invisible in GaAs (Ga and As have 31 and 33 electrons: 0.1% of the strongest peak) and strong in AlAs and InP (17% and 24%): the pattern reads the chemistry of the basis. And the splitting of a nearly lattice-matched film like AlAs on GaAs (0.13% mismatch) grows with tan θ, which is why epitaxial layers are measured on high-angle reflections. Caveats: atomic scattering factors are approximated by Z (no fall-off with angle, no Debye–Waller factor), so high-angle intensities are too large; real silicon shows a weak 'forbidden' (222) from its bonding charge; Kα2, absorption, preferred orientation and peak widths are ignored; COD entries were measured at different temperatures (thermal expansion shifts a by about 0.01% per 40 K in Si). Next: open a COD entry (click a peak), compare a measured pattern, or follow the lattice-matching example (chip-vegard-epitaxy) for alloys.

examples.title: Little's law in NumPy's CI
examples.description: Every GitHub Actions run of NumPy on one day, as intervals in Polars. examples.title: Codon usage bias: synonymous is not neutral
examples.description: 99 E. coli genes (Ensembl CDS, UniProt proteins): the genetic code read off the data, RSCU and Wright's Nc. Ribosomal proteins (median Nc 36.7) fall far below the mutation-only curve, regulators (51.3) stay near it: highly expressed genes use a preferred dialect of codons. Caveats: gene sets stand in for expression; short genes give noisy Nc.

catalog.title: Codon usage bias: synonymous is not neutral
catalog.summary: E. coli ribosomal proteins against regulators: the genetic code read from Ensembl DNA and UniProt proteins, RSCU and Wright's Nc show translational selection.
catalog.description: Question: the genetic code has 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids can be written several ways. Does a cell care which synonym it uses? Data: 99 Escherichia coli K-12 genes, their coding DNA from Ensembl and their proteins from UniProt: the 56 ribosomal proteins (among the most-made proteins in a growing cell) against 43 DNA-binding transcription regulators (made at a few copies per cell; the first 44 in genome order of UniProt's 304). Steps: each codon is paired with the residue at the same place in the protein, which reads the genetic code (64 codons, the degeneracy of each amino acid) off the two databases; then relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) per set, and per gene Wright's effective number of codons, Nc (20: one codon per amino acid, 61: all used equally), against the curve that mutation bias in G+C alone would give. The code comes out whole: all 64 codons, each opposite one amino acid (or stop) in every place but one (a TAA opposite Glu, an annotation difference). Aha: the regulators sit near the mutation-only curve (median Nc 51.3, 6 below it), while the ribosomal proteins fall far below it (median Nc 36.7, 23 below): they use a restricted dialect of preferred codons (Leu CTG, Arg CGT, Gly GGT; 63% of their synonymous codons against 36% in the regulators) and all but avoid the rare ones (RSCU of AGA 0.05, AGG 0, CTA 0.02, ATA 0.01, against 0.2–0.4 in the regulators). Synonymous is not neutral: selection for fast, accurate translation shapes the codons of highly expressed genes (Ikemura 1981, Sharp & Li 1987). Caveats: expression is not measured here, the gene sets stand for high and low expression; short genes give noisy Nc; the regulators were picked by genome order, not at random; ykgM is a paralogue of L31 made under zinc starvation, and cspE (a cold-shock protein) is abundant, so both sets have exceptions. tRNA gene copy numbers, the other half of the story, are not in this data. Next: hover a codon or a gene; drill into one amino acid's synonyms, or expand to another organism (Ensembl has yeast and human) or to measured protein abundance (PaxDb).

examples.title: Is dark energy weakening? DESI, supernovae and the Hubble tension
examples.description: Is dark energy weakening? DESI DR2's 2025 BAO distances, Pantheon+'s 1,701 supernovae and Planck's acoustic angle, fitted live on a grid of ΛCDM and evolving dark energy (w0, wa). Each ruler alone fits ΛCDM; together they disfavour it by 2.7σ (best w0 ≈ −0.87, wa ≈ −0.3), close to DESI's 2.8σ. The Hubble tension is separate: the distance ladder gives 73.2, the sound-wave ruler 68.8, Planck 67.4. Caveats: diagonal supernova errors, θ* alone for the CMB.

catalog.title: Is dark energy weakening? DESI, supernovae and the Hubble tension
catalog.summary: DESI DR2, Pantheon+ and the CMB fitted live: each ruler fits ΛCDM alone, together they disfavour it by 2.7σ. And the Hubble tension: 73 against 67–69.
catalog.description: Question: in March 2025 the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) reported that dark energy may be weakening: the cosmological constant of the standard model, ΛCDM, fits its map of 14 million galaxies and quasars less well than a dark energy that changes with time. How strong is that, and which data carry it? And is the "Hubble tension" the same problem? Data: DESI DR2's BAO distances (seven redshift bins, 13 numbers with their covariance; DESI collaboration via the Cobaya likelihood repository), the 1,701 type Ia supernovae of Pantheon+ with their SH0ES Cepheid calibration (Scolnic et al. 2022, Brout et al. 2022), and Planck's acoustic angle θ* and sound horizon. Steps: a flat universe of matter, radiation and dark energy with w(z) = w0 + wa·z/(1+z), integrated for 21 × 41 × 53 values of Ωm, w0 and wa (w0 + wa < 0); for each, the χ² of the BAO (scale c/(H0·r_d) fitted analytically), of the supernovae (their absolute brightness left free, Hubble-flow sample binned in 36 log-redshift bins), and of the CMB as one more distance, to z = 1090; then ΛCDM against the best (w0, wa) per combination, and H0 from the supernovae with Cepheid distances against H0 from the sound-horizon ruler. Aha: each ruler alone is consistent with ΛCDM (BAO 1.7σ, supernovae 0.3σ), but their allowed bands cross away from it: together ΛCDM is off by 2.7σ (Δχ² 10.2), best w0 ≈ −0.87, wa ≈ −0.3, close to DESI's own 2.8σ for DESI + CMB + Pantheon+ (w0 = −0.84, wa = −0.62 in their full analysis). The signal sits at z ≈ 0.5–0.7, where DESI's expansion rate runs 3% above ΛCDM. The Hubble tension is a separate fault line: the distance ladder gives H0 = 73.2 km/s/Mpc (statistical error only), the sound-wave ruler with Planck's r_d gives 68.8, Planck's ΛCDM 67.4 ± 0.5; changing late dark energy doesn't close it. Caveats: supernova errors are diagonal (the published 1,701 × 1,701 covariance with systematics isn't used), which makes them look stronger than they are; the CMB here is θ* alone, a weak stand-in for the full Planck likelihood (so BAO+CMB gives 1.5σ against DESI's 3.1σ); radiation and r*/r_d are fixed approximations; the grid is coarse (steps 0.01, 0.03, 0.08); the significance depends on which supernova sample is used (DESI: 2.8σ with Pantheon+, 4.2σ with DES-Y5). Next: hover any point; read a combination's Δχ² in the verdict table; drill into one BAO bin's tracer; expand to the DES-Y5 or Union3 supernovae, or the full CMB distance priors.

catalog.title: Influenza's R: exponential growth, herd immunity and final size
catalog.summary: US flu seasons (CDC FluView via Delphi): exponential growth on a log axis gives R of 1.1–1.3, then the SIR herd-immunity threshold and final size.
catalog.description: Question: how contagious is seasonal influenza, and what does that number imply? An epidemic in a susceptible population first grows exponentially, I(t) ∝ e^(rt), and the growth rate r together with the generation interval gives the reproduction number R. Data: CDC's US outpatient surveillance week by week since the 2016–17 season (Delphi Epidata: FluView wILI and the clinical labs' percent positive), combined into ILI+, the standard proxy for influenza incidence. Steps: per season the peak, the growth window (5–60% of the peak, before it) and r as the slope of ln(ILI+); then R = (1 + r·Tg/k)^k (Wallinga & Lipsitch, generation interval 3 days, gamma k = 4) and the SIR model's consequences: the herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R, the final size z = 1 − e^(−Rz) and the peak prevalence. Aha: on a log axis every season's rise is a straight line, and a gentle one: ILI+ doubles in 8 to 20 days (median about 14), which means an effective R of only 1.1–1.3 in the eight seasons fitted. Influenza spreads barely above the epidemic threshold: immunising or preventing 10–20% of transmissions stops growth, where measles (R0 12–18) needs over 90%. Yet even so small an R would infect 18–40% of a fully susceptible SIR population, about twice the threshold, because the epidemic overshoots it. Caveats: ILI+ is a proxy, not a count; R depends on the assumed generation interval; it is the effective R at the season's start (prior immunity, vaccination), not R0; seasons with two waves fit less well (read fit_r2); 2020–21 and 2021–22 had too little influenza to fit; SIR ignores school terms, age structure and behaviour; eight seasons are few for the study. Next: hover a week or a season; drill down to HHS regions or states (same API, regions=hhs1…hhs10); expand to subtypes or vaccination coverage.

catalog.summary: Chromosome 7's genes in the 3D domains Hi-C finds: a zoomable track, system › process › gene, organs, and domains holding one function (purity 0.68 against 0.44 shuffled).
catalog.description: Question: a chromosome folds into domains (TADs) that contact themselves more than their surroundings. Do the genes that share a domain also share a function, and where in the body are they used? Data: chromosome 7's protein-coding genes from the Human Protein Atlas (position on GRCh38, UniProt's biological-process and molecular-function keywords, RNA tissue specificity and nTPM in 19 tissues), and the contact domains Juicer's Arrowhead calls in GM12878 in situ Hi-C (ENCODE ENCFF203AKP; Rao et al. 2014), a gzipped BEDPE for all chromosomes. Steps: each gene's keywords grouped into a dozen systems; the domains nested (a domain inside a larger one gets it as parent) and each gene placed in the smallest domain that holds its middle; then, for the 31 domains with 3 or more annotated genes, the share of their genes in their most common system, against 1,000 shuffles of the systems anywhere on the chromosome and within 5 Mb. Aha: domains hold one function far more often than chance (mean purity 0.68 against 0.44 shuffled anywhere, p < 0.001), and still more than their neighbourhood alone gives (0.57 within 5 Mb, p < 0.001). The purest are tandem gene families: the T-cell receptor β and γ loci, a zinc-finger cluster at 64 Mb, HOXA2–6. HOXA9 sits between two domains, at the boundary that splits the HOXA cluster. Caveats: domains are from one cell line (a B-lymphoblastoid line), and boundaries differ between cell types; 438 of 1,002 genes have no UniProt process keyword; the grouping into systems is this board's; nTPM is RNA, not protein; only protein-coding genes are in HPA's list. Complexes: 164 of chromosome 7's genes are subunits of 445 curated complexes (Complex Portal, EBI), shown by family and function; a complex's PDB entry opens in 3D, its chains coloured by protein and this chromosome's subunits bright (RCSB, with PDBe's chain mapping). Curated complexes are a fraction of what binds: a gene missing there may still have partners. Next: set chrom to another chromosome; pin a gene for its card and links to HPA, Ensembl, GeneCards and Reactome; colour the track by organ; drill into a domain; expand to another cell line's domains (ENCODE has Hi-C for dozens).

examples.title: Gompertz's law: the risk of dying doubles about every seven years
examples.description: Eurostat life tables for eight countries, 2003 and 2023: from 35 to 84 the log death rate is a straight line, and the risk doubles every 6.6–10 years everywhere. Countries and decades differ in the level, not the rate of ageing (Strehler–Mildvan, r = −0.93). Off the line: the accident hump and the oldest ages.

catalog.title: Gompertz's law: the risk of dying doubles about every seven years
catalog.summary: Eurostat life tables, eight countries, 2003 and 2023: log death rate is linear in age 35–84, doubling every 6.6–10 years; levels differ, slopes barely.
catalog.description: Question: how does the risk of dying change with age? Gompertz (1825) proposed that adult death rates rise exponentially, m(x) = a·e^(bx), so that ln m(x) is a straight line in age. Is that so, and what differs between populations: the level a or the rate of ageing b? Data: Eurostat's life tables (demo_mlifetable), the death rate by single year of age for women and men in eight countries (Sweden, Denmark, France, Spain, Italy, Poland, Lithuania, Bulgaria), 2003 and 2023. Steps: ages as numbers and ln m(x); per country, sex and year a least-squares line over ages 35–84, giving b, the mortality-rate doubling time ln 2 / b, the level m(60) on the line and R²; each age's observed rate against the line; and per sex and year the spread of the doubling time against the spread of the level. Aha: from 35 to 84 the log death rate is a straight line (R² at least 0.985 in 2023), and the risk of dying doubles every 6.6 to 10 years (median about 7 for women, 7.5 for men), in every country. What differs is the level: m(60) is two to three times higher in Lithuania and Bulgaria than in Sweden or Spain, and it fell everywhere between 2003 and 2023 (Swedish men 8.9 to 5.9 per 1,000, Spanish men 11.1 to 6.7) while the doubling time barely moved. Where the level is low the slope is steeper (ln a and b correlate at −0.93 across the 16 lines of each year: the Strehler–Mildvan correlation), so populations postpone death more than they slow ageing. Off the line: infancy, the young-adult accident hump (up to five times the line at 18–25) and the oldest ages. Caveats: period life tables mix cohorts; the fitted range (35–84) is a choice and the open age group (85+ in 2003, 95+ in 2023) is left out; small countries' single-year rates are noisy at young ages (ten zero rates dropped); a is an extrapolation, not a newborn's risk. examples.title: Hardy–Weinberg, and why pooled populations break it
examples.description: Genotypes of five famous variants (LCT, SLC24A5, ALDH2, ACTN3, HbS) in 26 populations of 1000 Genomes (Ensembl, IGSR). Each population sits on the p², 2pq, q² parabola; pooled, heterozygotes vanish by exactly F_ST (SLC24A5: F 0.67 against 0.65), the Wahlund effect. HbS in Africa has too many heterozygotes: selection. catalog.title: Hardy–Weinberg, and why pooled populations break it
catalog.summary: Five variants in 26 populations of 1000 Genomes: each population on the Hardy–Weinberg parabola, pooled samples below it by F_ST (Wahlund effect).
catalog.description: Question: Hardy–Weinberg says that under random mating an allele at frequency p comes in genotypes p², 2pq and q², whatever p is. Do real human populations follow it, and what does it mean when they don't? Data: genotype counts for five well-known variants (rs4988235 lactase persistence, rs1426654 SLC24A5 skin pigmentation, rs671 ALDH2 alcohol flush, rs1815739 ACTN3 R577X, rs334 sickle-cell HbS) in the 26 populations of 1000 Genomes phase 3 (Ensembl REST), and the populations' sampling sites and super-populations (IGSR). Steps: per variant and sample, the allele frequency, the expected genotype counts, a chi-square test (1 df) and the heterozygote deficit F = 1 − H_obs/H_exp; then the Wahlund effect: for each pooled sample (all 26, or one super-population) the deficit predicted from the populations alone, F_ST = Var(p) / (p̄(1 − p̄)). Aha: single populations sit on the Hardy–Weinberg parabola (3 of 83 population tests at p < 0.05, all for ACTN3, about what chance gives), but pooling them makes heterozygotes vanish: all 2,504 people together have F = 0.67 for SLC24A5 (408 heterozygotes where 1,232 are expected), 0.39 for LCT and 0.20 for ALDH2, and F_ST from the populations predicts 0.65, 0.36 and 0.18. A departure from Hardy–Weinberg is a clue, not an error: here it is structure (a pooled sample is not one mating population). HbS goes the other way: no homozygotes among 661 Africans where 6.6 are expected (F = −0.11, p = 0.004), the mark of selection (sickle-cell disease against malaria protection for carriers), which in the pooled ALL sample cancels the Wahlund deficit (F = −0.03). Caveats: the variants were chosen for being famous, not at random; 61–113 people per population give the tests little power and some expected counts under 5; genotype calls have errors; sampling sites are where people were sampled (CEU in Utah). Next: hover any dot; add any rsID as another query; drill down to one super-population's populations; expand to selection scans or ancient DNA.

examples.title: Why did methane surge? Its budget, its short memory and its push on the climate
examples.description: Forty years of global methane (NOAA): the 2000–2006 pause, the record 2020–2022 surge, and the budget behind it. About 600 Tg are emitted and almost as much destroyed each year, so the record 2021 was an 8.5% imbalance. Its 9-year lifetime gives it a short memory: cut 30% by 2030 and it falls back to its 1980s level by 2050. ENSO explains about 1% of the wobble. Methane is 18% of the long-lived gases' forcing.

catalog.title: Why did methane surge? Its budget, its short memory and its push on the climate
catalog.summary: Global methane since 1983 (NOAA): the pause, the 2020–22 surge, a 600 Tg/yr budget where growth is a thin gap, and why cutting it works within a decade.
catalog.description: Question: methane is the second greenhouse gas after CO₂, and from 2020 to 2022 it rose faster than ever measured. Why does its growth swing so much, how big is the budget behind it, and what would cutting emissions do? Data: NOAA's globally averaged monthly methane at marine surface sites since 1983 with its de-seasonalised trend, NOAA's annual growth, NOAA's global CO₂ and N₂O, and NOAA CPC's Oceanic Niño Index. Steps: the monthly growth rate (the trend's 12-month change); ENSO against growth minus its 7-year mean at lags of −6 to 24 months; the budget in one box (emissions = 2.75 Tg/ppb × growth + stock ÷ a 9.1-year lifetime); three futures from today's emissions stepped monthly to 2060; and each gas's radiative forcing with Myhre et al.'s simplified formulas. Aha: growth is the thin difference between two huge flows. About 600 million tonnes are emitted a year and almost as much destroyed by OH; the record 2021 (17.7 ppb) was an 8.5% imbalance, and the 2000–2006 pause (0.5 ppb/yr) a balance. Because the air clears about a ninth of it every year, methane answers within a decade: held at 2025's emissions it levels off near 1,975 ppb, cut 30% by 2030 it falls back to about 1,430 ppb by 2050 (its 1980s level, 0.35 instead of 0.55 W/m²), while rising 1% a year takes it to 2,330 ppb. Nothing similar is possible with CO₂. ENSO, often blamed (La Niña wets tropical wetlands), explains only about 1% of the year-to-year wobble here (r = 0.10 with ENSO 10 months earlier). Methane is 18% of the three gases' 3.04 W/m² in 2025. Caveats: the one-box lifetime is uncertain (8.5–9.5 years) and fixed, whereas OH falls as methane rises (the perturbation lasts about 12 years) and fell in 2020's cleaner air; the 30% cut is applied to 2025's inferred emissions, not the pledge's 2020 baseline; the forcing is the direct one only (ozone and stratospheric water add about half again); a marine-site average misses regional sources; growth for the latest year is preliminary. Next: hover any month or year; drill down to a single station or latitude band (NOAA publishes both); expand to δ¹³C, the isotope that separates microbial from fossil sources, and to satellite (TROPOMI) maps of emitters.

examples.title: Which single changes break p53? AlphaMissense, gnomAD and ClinVar
examples.description: Every single amino-acid change in p53, three ways: AlphaMissense's prediction, how many of gnomAD's 807,000 people carry it, and ClinVar's verdict, with AlphaFold's fold in 3D. Harm sits in the folded core (74% likely pathogenic, 229 of 231 ClinVar pathogenic changes); the disordered ends tolerate almost anything. catalog.title: Which single changes break p53? AlphaMissense, gnomAD and ClinVar
catalog.summary: AlphaMissense, gnomAD and ClinVar on every possible p53 change, with AlphaFold in 3D: harm sits in the fold; prediction separates ClinVar's verdicts with AUC 0.99.
catalog.description: Question: p53, "the guardian of the genome", is the most often mutated gene in human cancer, and most of its cancer mutations swap a single amino acid. Of the 7,467 possible single swaps in its 393 residues, which ones break it? Can a model tell before any patient carries them, and do evolution and the clinic agree? Data: AlphaMissense's prediction for every swap (Google DeepMind, Cheng et al., Science 2023; 0 benign … 1 pathogenic), on the protein and on GRCh38; AlphaFold's model and per-residue confidence (pLDDT); gnomAD v4's allele counts in about 807,000 people; and ClinVar's classifications through gnomAD's API. Steps: the swaps one DNA letter can make (2,314) joined to gnomAD and ClinVar by genomic variant, not by protein name (the two name changes on different transcripts); then AlphaMissense by how common a change is, against ClinVar's reviewed classifications, and per residue against AlphaFold's confidence. Aha: harm is a property of the fold. The DNA-binding core (pLDDT ≥ 90, 207 residues) holds 74% likely-pathogenic swaps and 229 of the 231 ClinVar pathogenic ones; the disordered ends (pLDDT < 50, 117 residues) tolerate almost anything (7%). AlphaMissense ranks reviewed pathogenic above benign with AUC 0.989 (97% of 224 pathogenic called likely pathogenic, 83% of 144 benign called likely benign), and would call 37% of the 555 variants of uncertain significance pathogenic and 52% benign. The commoner a change in people, the more benign: median score 0.41 for changes seen in one person, 0.14 for rare ones, 0.07 for those above 1 in 10,000. Caveats: the "one person" band scores higher than never-seen changes because gnomAD's blood samples carry clonal haematopoiesis (TP53 mutations acquired with age), not only inherited variants; AlphaMissense learnt from human and primate population frequencies, so agreement with gnomAD is partly by construction, while ClinVar is the independent test (though recent classifications may cite it, and TP53's lean on functional assays); the model and the scores are for one chain alone, without DNA, zinc or partners; the files are AlphaFold's model v6. Next: hover any cell of the map; click a residue to see it in 3D; set gene and uniprot together to another protein (BRCA1 P38398, KRAS P01116, CFTR P13569, PTEN P60484); filter the changes table to ClinVar uncertain.

catalog.summary: Why doubling fertiliser doesn't double the harvest: a Mitscherlich yield-response curve fitted to 136 countries, the grain each extra kg buys, and who sits on the flat part.
catalog.description: Question: why does the world not simply double its harvest by doubling fertiliser? World Bank (FAO) fertiliser use per hectare of arable land and cereal yields for about 180 countries; Polars fits Mitscherlich's law Y = Y0 + A(1 − e^(−cN)) by grid search with a profile-likelihood interval, computes each country's marginal product and residual, the grain each successive 50 kg/ha buys, and eight countries' paths since 2000. Aha: half the response comes in the first ~54 kg/ha; past ~300 kg/ha one more kilogram returns about a kilogram of grain, the rest is lost as nitrate and N₂O. A study tests the rise, the falling grain per kg and irrigation's share. Caveats: cross-country confounding (climate, irrigation, seeds), all three nutrients per arable hectare, differing latest years.

catalog.title: The Ramachandran plot: why proteins have helices and sheets
catalog.summary: φ and ψ of 606 residues of four proteins (PDBe): half lie in 1.4% of the plane; helices and strands are the allowed basins, positive φ is glycine's.
catalog.description: Question: a protein backbone has two free rotations per residue, φ (around N–Cα) and ψ (around Cα–C). Why do proteins fold into a few repeating shapes, helices and sheets, rather than anything at all? Data: the backbone angles of every residue of four well-resolved proteins, myoglobin 1A6M (1.0 Å, all α), T4 lysozyme 2LZM, ubiquitin 1UBQ and green fluorescent protein 1EMA (a β-barrel), as PDBe's validation pipeline (MolProbity) computed them from the coordinates, with PDBe's helix and strand assignments. Steps: residues with φ and ψ per entry, joined to the helix and strand ranges; each residue placed in a region of the plane (α_R, β, PPII, α_L) and in a 10° cell; then the occupancy of the plane, and summaries per secondary structure and for glycine and proline apart. Aha: only a small part of the 360° × 360° square is used, because atoms of neighbouring residues collide everywhere else (Ramachandran, 1963): half of the 606 residues lie in 1.4% of the plane and 95% in 10.6% (10° cells). Helix residues sit in one tight basin (median φ −64°, ψ −40°), strands in another (−120°, +135°); positive φ is glycine's (22 of the 34 residues there; 48% of glycines against 2% of other residues), the one amino acid without a side chain, and proline's ring pins φ at −63° ± 10°. Secondary structure is a run of residues in one basin. Caveats: four proteins (606 residues; alternate conformations, listed twice with the same angles, counted once) are a small sample; the region boxes are approximate (MolProbity's Favored/Allowed contours come from ~100,000 residues and differ per residue type); PDBe's helix/strand ranges come from the deposited annotation; angles are from crystal structures (one conformation). Next: hover a residue; drill down to one protein or residue type; expand to more PDB entries (any id works with the same queries) or to NMR ensembles.

examples.title: Reproduce Figure 1: near-stasis in Mesozoic tetrapods
examples.description: Question: does a published diversity curve still stand when it is rebuilt from today's data? Benson et al. 2016 (PLOS Biology, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002359) counted the non-marine tetrapods of the Mesozoic in the Paleobiology Database and found near-stasis: no long-term trend in genus or species counts unless the first Triassic bin is left out (their Figure 1), and a net diversification rate near zero after subsampling (Figure 5). This board rebuilds Figure 1B–C live from the PBDB, next to a link to the original figure, with the paper's Poisson trend lines, shareholder quorum subsampling (quorum 0.4), the paper's numbers beside today's and a study of the claim. Click a bin for the PBDB records behind it. Caveats: PBDB's 10-Myr bins and terrestrial filter approximate the paper's bins and taxon list; the PBDB has grown since 2015; this SQS is global and at genus level, the paper's regional and at species level. Cite the board, the paper and the PBDB from the Cite panel; Copy as Python reruns the pipeline.

examples.title: Upcoming rocket launches

Statistics: Poisson waiting times. If launches came at random at a steady rate, the gaps between them would be exponential, a straight line on a log axis; the last 100 launches are compared with that model, with the rate per day and the chance of a day without a launch. examples.title: Ukraine: front, forces and odds
examples.description: Question: who is gaining ground in Ukraine, where are the forces, and what do markets give for a ceasefire, a peace deal or territorial concessions by a given month? The map lays DeepStateMap's areas of control (now, and the line of 1 January 2026 dashed) on GMRT terrain, with its attack directions, the Russian units and airfields it places, and 120 days of its located updates (each a place it reports changing hands). The area step measures the net change in km² since 1 January; the weekly chart counts reported advances by side. The odds chart is the ontology's 'outcome by deadline': each Polymarket 'by ...?' event is a probability curve over its deadlines (a cumulative distribution), so you can read the chance of a ceasefire before a month and year; Manifold adds play-money forecasts; UN News and GDELT the diplomacy. Caveats: DeepStateMap is a Ukrainian volunteer project (sources: its own, the General Staff, geolocated footage); its unit positions are its placements, not verified here, and a quiet sector is unreported rather than unchanged. Market prices are not probabilities (fees, thin trading; hollow dots break the ordering). GDELT allows one request every 5 seconds per address and may refuse: rerun it. Terrain is about 7 km per cell.
